questions.prompt: Standard reduction potentials are Cu2++2e−→Cu, +0.34 V, and Zn2++2e−→Zn, −0.76 V. What is E°cell for Zn+Cu2+→Zn2++Cu?
questions.explanation: C is correct. E°cell=E°red,cathode−E°red,anode=0.34−(−0.76)=1.10 V. A is incorrect: that adds both reduction potentials without reversing zinc. B is incorrect: that is the reverse reaction potential. D is incorrect: that subtracts magnitudes rather than signed reduction potentials.

questions.prompt: For Cu(s)+2Ag+(aq)→Cu2+(aq)+2Ag(s), E°cell=0.46 V. Use F=96485 C/mol e−. What is ΔG° per equation as written?
questions.explanation: A is correct. Two electrons transfer, so ΔG°=−2(96485)(0.46)=−88766 J. B is incorrect: that uses one electron instead of two. C is incorrect: that loses the negative sign in−nFE°. D is incorrect: that converts the number to kJ but retains J units.

questions.prompt: For2Al+3Cu2+→2Al3++3Cu, use reduction potentials−1.66 V for Al3+/Al and+0.34 V for Cu2+/Cu. Which E°cell and electron count are correct?
questions.explanation: B is correct. The potential difference is0.34−(−1.66)=2.00 V. Balancing two three-electron oxidations with three two-electron reductions transfers six electrons. A is incorrect: reduction potentials are not multiplied by balancing coefficients. C is incorrect: electron count is balanced transfer, not the sum of individual ion charges3+2. D is incorrect: that gives the opposite redox direction.

questions.prompt: A standard cell reaction transfers2 mol electrons per stated reaction amount and has E°=+0.500 V. With F=96485 C/mol, what is ΔG°?
questions.explanation: D is correct. −nFE°=−2×96485×0.500=−96485 J. A is incorrect: positive cell potential gives negative standard free-energy change. B is incorrect: that omits the factor two. C is incorrect: that omits multiplication by0.500 V.

questions.prompt: A balanced redox equation has n=3 and ΔG°=−28.9455 kJ. Use F=96485 C/mol. What is E°cell?
questions.explanation: A is correct. E°=−ΔG°/(nF)=28945.5/(3×96485)=0.100. B is incorrect: that fails to apply the leading minus sign. C is incorrect: that omits n in the denominator. D is incorrect: that fails to convert kJ to J.

questions.prompt: For the intended standard redox direction, E°cell=−0.20 V. What does this imply?
options: ΔG° is negative because any voltage implies favorability
The direction must be self-powered under standard conditions
ΔG° is positive, so that direction requires external driving under standard conditions.
questions.explanation: C is correct. With n and F positive,−nFE° is positive when E° is negative. A is incorrect: the cell-potential sign matters. B is incorrect: negative E° opposes that interpretation. D is incorrect: thermodynamic unfavorability is not a balancing defect.

questions.prompt: Every coefficient of a balanced redox equation is doubled. At the same standard conditions, how do E°cell and ΔG° change?
options: E°cell doubles and ΔG° stays unchanged
E°cell is unchanged and ΔG° doubles.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Voltage is intensive; transferred electron amount and free-energy change scale with the equation amount. A is incorrect: potential is not multiplied by stoichiometric scale. B is incorrect: the extensive and intensive behaviors are reversed. C is incorrect: coefficient scaling does not reverse direction.

questions.prompt: A standard cell reaction has E°=+0.75 V. What is the standard potential for the exactly reversed reaction?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Reversal changes the sign of the driving potential and standard free-energy change. A is incorrect: that leaves the redox direction unchanged. C is incorrect: voltage is not inverted on reversal. D is incorrect: reversal does not eliminate the endpoint free-energy difference.

questions.prompt: Standard reduction potentials for M2+/M and N2+/N are+0.60 V and−0.20 V. Which pairing gives the favorable standard cell direction?
options: Reduce N2+ and oxidize M, giving E°cell=+0.80 V
Reduce both M2+ and N2+ without any oxidation
Add the listed reductions to get E°cell=+0.40 V
Reduce M2+ and oxidize N, giving E°cell=+0.80 V.
questions.explanation: D is correct. The more positive reduction is paired with the reverse of the less positive reduction. A is incorrect: that direction actually gives−0.80 V. B is incorrect: a complete cell reaction requires an electron source. C is incorrect: one half-reaction must be reversed to balance electrons.

questions.prompt: Why are standard reduction potentials not multiplied when half-reaction coefficients are scaled to balance electrons?
options: Scaling changes both free energy and transferred charge proportionally, leaving their ratio unchanged.
Because electron conservation is unnecessary in a cell
Because free energy never scales with reaction amount
Because all standard reduction potentials are equal
questions.explanation: A is correct. E°=−ΔG°/(nF) is unchanged when numerator and electron amount scale together. B is incorrect: electron conservation is still required. C is incorrect: free energy is extensive and does scale. D is incorrect: different half-reactions have different potentials.

questions.prompt: A balanced standard cell reaction has E°cell>0. Which thermodynamic pair follows?
options: ΔG°<0 and K>1 for that equation at that temperature.
questions.explanation: C is correct. The cell relation gives negative ΔG°; the equilibrium relation−RTlnK then implies K>1. A is incorrect: both signs correspond to the opposite standard direction. B is incorrect: that requires zero standard potential. D is incorrect: equilibrium favorability does not guarantee fast or exactly complete conversion.
